SRA enumerators are starting weekly reports from cities across Somalia.

How the data is collected

SRA enumerators record the pump price at stations in each city, usually every Sunday. Each city's weekly price is the median of all reports from that city in the week (Monday to Sunday), so one unusual station does not move the figure. Reports that differ by more than 20% from the previous week are checked by SRA before they are published. Free to use with credit: Source: Somali Researchers Association (SRA), Fuel Price Tracker.

Protecting Participants and Promoting Responsible Research

The Somali Researchers Association Research Ethics Committee (SRA-REC) reviews research involving human participants to help protect their rights, dignity, safety, privacy and well-being.

The Committee supports research that is ethically responsible, scientifically sound and appropriate to Somalia’s social and cultural context. Its review process is guided by internationally recognised research ethics principles and relevant national requirements.

Role of the Committee

The Committee reviews research proposals and supporting documents to assess:

  • The purpose and ethical justification of the research
  • Potential risks and expected benefits
  • Participant recruitment and selection
  • Informed-consent procedures
  • Privacy, confidentiality and data protection
  • Inclusion of children and other potentially vulnerable groups
  • Participant compensation or reimbursement
  • Cultural and community considerations
  • The qualifications and responsibilities of the research team
  • Plans for storing, using, sharing and disposing of research data

The Committee may also review important changes made to an approved study and ethical concerns reported during its implementation.

Committee Composition

The SRA Research Ethics Committee brings together professionals with relevant knowledge and experience in areas such as:

  • Research methods
  • Public health and medicine
  • Social and behavioural sciences
  • Ethics and law
  • Data protection
  • Community and participant perspectives

External specialists may be consulted when a proposal requires expertise that is not available within the Committee.

Independence and Conflicts of Interest

Committee members are expected to review applications fairly, objectively and confidentially. Members must declare any actual or potential conflict of interest and must not participate in decisions where their independence could reasonably be questioned.

Research commissioned, managed or conducted by SRA is subject to the same ethical-review requirements as research submitted by external applicants.

Possible Review Decisions

Following its review, the Committee may:

  • Approve the research
  • Approve it subject to specified conditions
  • Request revisions or additional information
  • Defer a decision pending further clarification
  • Decline approval where ethical concerns have not been adequately addressed

Applicants receive written communication explaining the Committee’s decision and any actions required.

Confidentiality

Research proposals, personal information and Committee discussions are handled confidentially. Information is accessed only by Committee members, authorised administrative staff and specialist reviewers involved in the assessment.

Apply for Ethical Review

Researchers, universities, government institutions, NGOs, development partners and private organizations conducting research involving human participants in Somalia may apply for ethical review.

To begin an application, visit the Apply for Ethical Approval page or contact sra@sra.so.

The SRA Research Ethics Committee reviews studies involving human participants in Somalia: surveys, interviews, focus groups, clinical and programme research. You get a clear, written decision, on time for your fieldwork.

Please note: SRA ethical approval is an independent institutional review. It does not replace any permission or approval required by federal or state authorities. Clinical trials and certain health studies may also require approval from the Ministry of Health or the Somali National Institute of Health.

Who we review for

Funders, universities and journals increasingly require local ethical approval for research carried out in Somalia. SRA provides it for:

◎

International research & evaluation firms

Baselines, endlines, household surveys and qualitative studies for donor-funded programmes.

✚

NGOs and humanitarian agencies

Needs assessments, programme research and studies with displaced or vulnerable communities.

♥

Hospitals and clinical teams

Hospital-based and clinical studies by doctors and health researchers.

✎

Universities and students

Master’s and PhD research by students of Somali and foreign universities collecting data in Somalia.

How it works

A short, structured process. Apply before data collection starts: approval is not issued retrospectively.

Request the form

Email sra@sra.so. You receive the institutional or student application form.

Submit your study

Return the completed form with your proposal, questionnaire or tools, and consent forms.

Committee review

We check the application and contact you if anything needs clarifying. Higher-risk studies receive a fuller review.

Written decision

You receive a signed decision letter: approval, approval with conditions, or requested revisions.

What the Committee looks at

Participant protection

  • Purpose and ethical justification of the study
  • Risks and expected benefits
  • Recruitment and selection of participants
  • Children and other groups needing extra protection
  • Compensation or reimbursement

Consent, privacy and context

  • Informed consent: written, oral or electronic, and in Somali
  • Privacy, confidentiality and data protection
  • Data shared with other organisations or transferred abroad
  • Cultural and community considerations
  • Qualifications of the research team

Why researchers choose SRA

Local knowledge

Reviewers understand Somalia’s communities, languages and fieldwork realities, so the review improves your study rather than delaying it.

Independent and confidential

Members declare conflicts of interest, and proposals and tools are kept confidential. SRA’s own studies go through the same review.

Practical support

Need your consent form or questionnaire in Somali? SRA also offers translation and data collection.

Common questions

Can I apply after data collection has started?

No. Ethical approval is not normally issued retrospectively once data collection or analysis has begun. Apply as early as possible in your planning.

Do I also need government approval?

SRA ethical approval is an independent institutional review. It does not replace any permission or approval required by federal or state authorities. Clinical trials and certain health studies may also require approval from the Ministry of Health or the Somali National Institute of Health. Where a study needs both, apply to SRA and to the relevant authority; mention any existing approvals in your application.

What documents do I need?

The completed application form, your research proposal or concept note, data collection tools (questionnaire, interview or focus-group guides) and consent forms. See the full requirements.

My study already has approval from another institution. Do I still need SRA approval?

Many funders and partners require approval from a body in the country where data is collected. Mention any existing approval in your application; it helps the Committee’s review.

Is there a fee?

Yes, a review fee applies, depending on the type of study and applicant. Email sra@sra.so for a quotation.

Who sits on the Committee?

Read about the Committee’s membership, independence and decision process on About the Committee.

Case Study 1: Nationwide Health-Facility Assessment

Sector: Health
Year: 2026
Geographic coverage: Banadir and Federal Member States
Facilities assessed: 31
Assignment type: Facility audit and service-readiness assessment

The Challenge

Reliable information was needed to understand whether selected health facilities had the systems, resources and arrangements required to provide the assessed services.

The assignment required consistent data from facilities operating in different locations and conditions. It also required careful handling of sensitive health-service information.

SRA’s Approach

SRA developed and implemented a standardised assessment across 31 health facilities.

The work included:

  • Reviewing assessment indicators and tools
  • Training field researchers
  • Conducting facility visits
  • Interviewing responsible health personnel
  • Reviewing available records and service documentation
  • Observing infrastructure and service arrangements
  • Applying digital data-quality checks
  • Validating findings before reporting

The same core assessment standards were applied across all locations to make the findings comparable.

What the Assessment Examined

The assessment reviewed areas including:

  • Service availability and operating arrangements
  • Staffing and staff preparedness
  • Availability of protocols and guidance
  • Privacy and confidentiality arrangements
  • Referral and follow-up systems
  • Availability of essential supplies
  • Documentation and record management
  • Access to information and support services

Value Delivered

The assignment provided a structured national picture of facility readiness and identified differences in service availability, documentation, staff preparation and infrastructure.

SRA presented the findings with practical recommendations to help the responsible institutions prioritise improvements, strengthen service standards and monitor future progress.

Case Study 2: Strengthening the Quality of School Data

Sector: Education
Year: 2023
Assignment type: Data-quality assessment
Focus: School and programme information

The Challenge

Reliable school data is essential for programme planning, monitoring and reporting. The assignment required an assessment of whether information collected from participating schools was complete, accurate, consistent and suitable for decision-making.

SRA’s Approach

SRA reviewed the available datasets, reporting tools, school records and data-management processes.

The assessment included:

  • Reviewing indicator definitions
  • Comparing reported figures with available source records
  • Checking for missing information and duplicate entries
  • Examining consistency between related variables
  • Reviewing reporting processes and responsibilities
  • Discussing data-quality challenges with relevant personnel
  • Documenting identified gaps and corrective recommendations

What the Assessment Examined

The assessment considered:

  • Accuracy of reported information
  • Completeness of school records
  • Consistency across different reporting tools
  • Timeliness of data submission
  • Clarity of indicator definitions
  • Data storage and management procedures
  • Internal verification and quality-control practices

Value Delivered

The assessment identified weaknesses affecting the reliability and use of school data. SRA provided recommendations for improving reporting tools, strengthening verification procedures and clarifying data-management responsibilities.

The findings helped establish a clearer basis for programme reporting and future education planning.

Humanitarian Research, Monitoring and Evaluation

Reliable Evidence for Effective Humanitarian Response

Somali Researchers Association (SRA) provides research, needs assessment, monitoring and evaluation services to organisations responding to humanitarian needs in Somalia.

We support humanitarian agencies, government institutions and development partners to understand affected communities’ needs, verify the delivery of assistance, measure programme results and improve accountability to beneficiaries.

Our work considers Somalia’s complex humanitarian context, including drought, flooding, displacement, food insecurity, conflict, limited access to essential services and the different needs of vulnerable population groups.

SRA can support research and assessments in areas including:

  • Humanitarian needs and vulnerability
  • Internal displacement and durable solutions
  • Food security and livelihoods
  • Cash and voucher assistance
  • Health and nutrition

  • Protection and safeguarding

  • Climate-related emergencies
  • Emergency preparedness and response

  • Humanitarian access and service coverage
  • Accountability to affected populations
  • Gender, disability and social inclusion
  • Localisation and community-led response

How We Support Humanitarian Programmes

Humanitarian Needs Assessments

SRA conducts rapid and detailed assessments to identify priority needs, service gaps and vulnerable population groups. Assessments may examine access to food, water, shelter, healthcare, education, protection and livelihood opportunities.

Third-Party Monitoring

We independently verify whether humanitarian activities are being implemented as reported. Monitoring may include site visits, beneficiary interviews, observation, document review, GPS verification and photographic evidence where appropriate.

Post-Distribution Monitoring

SRA collects feedback from people who have received cash, vouchers, food, non-food items or other assistance. This helps clients understand whether assistance was received, used safely and appropriately, and met beneficiaries’ priority needs.

Programme Monitoring and Evaluation

We support baseline studies, real-time reviews, mid-term evaluations, final evaluations and outcome assessments of humanitarian and early-recovery programmes.

Beneficiary Feedback and Accountability

SRA conducts community consultations, satisfaction surveys, perception studies and interviews to understand beneficiaries’ experiences, concerns and recommendations.

Facility and Service Verification

Our teams can verify humanitarian service points, distribution sites, schools, health facilities, water points and other supported infrastructure. Verification may assess functionality, accessibility, utilisation and compliance with agreed standards.

Market and Price Monitoring

We collect and analyse market information to help clients understand prices, product availability, supply conditions and the purchasing power of households receiving cash or voucher assistance.

Our Methods

Depending on the assignment, SRA may use:

  • Rapid and multi-sector needs assessments
  • Household and beneficiary surveys
  • Digital data collection using CAPI and CATI
  • Key informant interviews
  • Focus group discussions
  • Direct observation and facility verification
  • Post-distribution monitoring
  • GPS and photographic verification
  • Market and price assessments
  • Document and programme-data reviews
  • GIS and service-coverage mapping
  • Case studies and outcome monitoring

Responsible Research in Crisis Settings

SRA applies conflict-sensitive and do-no-harm approaches when working with crisis-affected communities. Participation is voluntary, informed consent is obtained, and personal information is managed confidentially.

Our teams receive assignment-specific guidance on safeguarding, respectful engagement, data protection and the inclusion of women, children, persons with disabilities, displaced populations and other groups that may face additional barriers.

Typical Deliverables

Our humanitarian assignments may produce:

  • Humanitarian needs-assessment reports
  • Third-party monitoring reports
  • Post-distribution monitoring reports
  • Baseline, mid-term and final evaluation reports
  • Beneficiary-feedback and satisfaction reports
  • Facility and activity-verification reports
  • Market and price-monitoring reports
  • Cleaned and validated datasets
  • Maps, dashboards and visual summaries
  • Corrective-action recommendations
  • Briefings and presentations for decision-makers

Local Knowledge and Nationwide Reach

SRA combines humanitarian research experience with a nationwide field network. Our locally recruited teams understand community structures, local languages, cultural practices and operating conditions across Somalia.

Field deployment is planned according to accessibility, security conditions, ethical requirements and the needs of each assignment.

Climate Resilience and Disaster Risk Research

Evidence for Climate-Resilient Communities and Institutions

Somali Researchers Association (SRA) provides research, assessment, monitoring and data services to organisations working on climate change, disaster-risk reduction and community resilience in Somalia.

We support government institutions, development partners and civil society organisations to understand climate and disaster risks, identify vulnerable communities, assess resilience programmes and develop evidence-based responses.

Our work considers Somalia’s exposure to drought, floods, environmental degradation, water scarcity, displacement and livelihood disruption.

Our Research Areas

SRA can support research and assessments in areas including:

  • Drought and flood risk
  • Climate vulnerability and adaptation
  • Disaster preparedness and response
  • Community resilience and coping capacity
  • Climate-related displacement
  • Water scarcity and water-resource management
  • Food security and nutrition
  • Agriculture and climate-smart farming
  • Pastoral livelihoods and livestock systems
  • Environmental degradation and natural-resource management
  • Urban resilience and infrastructure
  • Climate-related health and education risks
  • Gender, disability and social inclusion
  • Climate finance and disaster-risk financing
  • Institutional capacity for climate and disaster management

How We Support Climate and Resilience Programmes

Climate and Disaster Risk Assessments

SRA examines hazards, exposure, vulnerability and coping capacity to identify who and what may be at risk. Assessments can be conducted at national, state, district or community level.

District and Community Risk Profiles

We support the preparation of practical profiles that bring together climate, environmental, demographic, infrastructure and livelihood information. These profiles can identify priority risks, vulnerable groups and geographic hotspots.

Resilience and Adaptation Research

SRA studies how households, communities, institutions and businesses prepare for, respond to and recover from climate shocks. Findings can support adaptation strategies, resilience programmes and resource allocation.

Programme Monitoring and Evaluation

We provide baseline studies, mid-term reviews, final evaluations and third-party monitoring of climate adaptation, disaster-risk reduction, food-security, livelihoods and resilience programmes.

Community and Stakeholder Consultation

Our teams engage government institutions, district administrations, community leaders, women, young people, pastoralists, farmers, displaced populations and other affected groups.

These consultations help explain local hazard history, livelihood changes, existing coping mechanisms and community priorities.

GIS and Risk Mapping

SRA can combine field-collected information with available geographic, administrative and environmental datasets to produce maps showing hazards, exposure, vulnerability, services and priority risk areas.

Where an assignment requires specialised climate modelling or remote-sensing analysis, SRA works with appropriately qualified technical specialists.

Our Methods

Depending on the assignment, SRA may use:

  • Review of climate, disaster and environmental datasets
  • Household and community surveys
  • Key informant interviews
  • Focus group discussions
  • Historical hazard and event analysis
  • Vulnerability and coping-capacity assessments
  • Institutional and policy reviews
  • GPS field verification
  • GIS and spatial analysis
  • Available satellite and remote-sensing information
  • Participatory community mapping
  • Stakeholder consultations and validation workshops

Climate-risk findings are presented with clear explanations of the data sources, assumptions and limitations.

Typical Deliverables

Our climate and resilience assignments may produce:

  • Climate and disaster-risk assessment reports

The Cost of Living Pressure Index (CLPI) helps explain how changes in prices and living costs are affecting people’s daily lives. Rather than focusing only on numbers, CLPI looks at whether households can still afford basic needs and how they cope when costs rise.

CLPI is not an inflation rate and not an official government index. It is an independent, research-based tool developed by the Somali Researchers Association (SRA) to reflect lived economic realities.

CLPI focuses on everyday pressures that families face including the cost of food, transport, fuel, housing, water, healthcare, and education and whether household income is enough to cover these needs throughout the month. It also considers common coping behaviors, such as reducing consumption or borrowing to manage expenses.

This index matters because prices alone do not always tell the full story. Even when markets appear stable, many households may feel increasing financial strain. CLPI helps highlight early signs of stress and changes in affordability over time, providing useful context for public discussion, research, and development planning.

Through CLPI, SRA shares clear and easy-to-understand signals about cost-of-living pressure, focusing on trends and direction rather than technical figures. The aim is to support better understanding of economic conditions while complementing not replacing official economic data.

Somali Researchers Association (SRA) believes that researchers, academics and students have the right to investigate, analyse, discuss, publish and share facts, figures and research findings without intimidation, censorship, discrimination or unlawful interference. No researcher should be threatened, detained, dismissed or punished for conducting responsible research or sharing evidence in accordance with professional and ethical standards.

To support this right, SRA documents, assesses and monitors serious incidents affecting academic freedom and the human rights of members of the research and academic community. These incidents may include:

  • Killings, threats and physical violence

  • Enforced disappearances

  • Arbitrary or unlawful detention

  • Restrictions on travel or freedom of movement

  • Dismissal or loss of an academic position

  • Expulsion or suspension from study

  • Censorship or restriction of research and publication

  • Intimidation, harassment and other serious violations

The information collected helps SRA understand the risks facing researchers, raise public and institutional awareness, and support the development of more effective responses.

SRA handles reported cases responsibly, respects confidentiality and seeks to verify information before using it for documentation, referral, advocacy or public reporting.

Written work and transcripts are priced per word. Interpretation, including telephone interviews, events and speeches, is priced per hour. Send us your document or event details and we will send a written quotation.

How long does it take?

It depends on the length and the subject. We agree the delivery date with you before we start.

What files can I send?

Send your documents, audio or video files and tell us the format you want back. We deliver in the format you need.

Is my material kept confidential?

Yes. Your documents and recordings are handled confidentially, shared only with the team working on them, and not used for any other purpose.

Do you also collect the data?

Yes. SRA also runs data collection and ethical review, so tools translated by us can go straight to the field.

Somali Researchers Association (SRA) provides independent third-party monitoring services to help clients verify project implementation, service delivery, beneficiary reach and compliance with agreed standards.

Our monitoring provides clients with reliable evidence about what is happening at project sites, including whether activities have been implemented, facilities and assets are available and functional, intended beneficiaries are receiving services, and reported results are supported by field evidence.

Monitoring Design

At the beginning of each assignment, SRA develops a detailed third-party monitoring plan that defines:

  • Monitoring questions and indicators

  • Data sources and verification methods

  • Locations and project sites to be monitored

  • Sampling and respondent-selection procedures

  • Monitoring frequency and reporting timelines

  • Data-collection tools and quality checks

  • Data-disaggregation requirements

  • Analysis and reporting plans

  • Procedures for escalating urgent findings

The monitoring approach is adapted to the programme, sector, geographic coverage, local context and client requirements.

Field Monitoring

SRA deploys trained field monitors, supervisors and regional coordinators through its nationwide field network. Field monitors may use Android smartphones or tablets with digital data-collection platforms such as SurveyCTO or other client-approved systems.

Where required and ethically appropriate, digital monitoring tools may include GPS coordinates, timestamps and photographic evidence to support the verification of reported activities and outputs.

Field teams receive assignment-specific training covering:

  • Monitoring tools and indicators

  • Interviewing and observation techniques

  • Informed consent

  • Safeguarding and do-no-harm principles

  • Data protection, security and confidentiality

  • Photographic and GPS-verification protocols

  • Reporting and escalation procedures

Context Monitoring

In hard-to-reach or security-constrained locations, changes in the operating environment can affect project implementation, access and beneficiary outcomes. SRA therefore incorporates contextual monitoring where relevant.

Structured contextual-monitoring tools may cover:

  • Security and accessibility conditions

  • Population movements and displacement

  • Health emergencies and disease outbreaks

  • Droughts, floods and other natural hazards

  • Market and service disruptions

  • Humanitarian and development activities

  • Changes affecting project sites or beneficiaries

This information helps clients understand whether changes in the local context have affected programme delivery or the reliability of reported results.

Facility and Project-Site Verification

For each assignment, SRA can develop and maintain an assignment-specific database of relevant schools, healthcare facilities, infrastructure sites, community projects and other service-delivery locations.

Field observations may be triangulated with beneficiary interviews, administrative records, stakeholder consultations, GPS information and photographic evidence.

Quality Assurance and Reporting

SRA applies quality controls throughout the monitoring process, including:

  • Daily review of submitted data

  • Supervisor checks and respondent back-checks

  • GPS, timestamp and photographic verification

  • Review of missing or inconsistent responses

  • Triangulation of evidence from different sources

  • Immediate escalation of critical findings

  • Preparation of monitoring reports and dashboards

Our reports present verified findings, identified gaps, emerging risks and practical recommendations to support timely client decision-making and programme improvement.

WHO WE ARE · SINCE 2010

Somali research, by Somali researchers, for better decisions

The Somali Researchers Association (SRA) is an independent research, monitoring and data organisation based in Mogadishu. Through a network of Somali researchers and trained enumerators, we collect reliable data across Somalia and turn it into evidence for government, UN agencies, NGOs, universities and businesses.

Why clients work with SRA

International agencies and local institutions choose SRA when they need data they can trust from places that are hard to reach.

Local reach, everywhere in Somalia

Our enumerators live in the communities they survey. They speak the language, understand the context and can work where outside teams cannot.

Quality you can check

Field teams use tablets with SurveyCTO and GPS. Every dataset is checked before analysis, and monitors are trained in informed consent, data security and confidentiality.

Independent and ethical

We work independently and objectively. SRA runs its own Research Ethics Committee, and our own studies go through the same review.

Delivered to plan

We work closely with clients and communities, and deliver to the terms of reference, budget and timeline agreed. Reports come in English, with Somali versions on request.
